She has one further observation, offered without much comfort. If the cooperative had been given only the sound record, and had been told what the sound record was supposed to mean, it would have concluded in 2019 that the closure had failed. The closure was the thing that worked.

title: The Sweep
text:
Every public library in the state reports one number to the body that funds it, and that number is circulation: how many items left the building on somebody’s card. It is cheap to collect, hard to argue with, and it has shaped what libraries buy for forty years.

In 2014 the Kettleman County system, which runs a main branch and four small ones, began counting something else alongside it. Staff walked the floor four times a day on a fixed schedule and wrote down, on a clipboard, every item they found sitting on a table, a study carrel, or the arm of a chair — anything a person had taken off a shelf and not checked out. They called it the sweep.

The sweep was not invented in Kettleman. The method is ordinary in library work. What was unusual was that Kettleman kept it up for nine years and published what it found.

The two records disagree, and they disagree by collection. For popular fiction, circulation and sweep counts rise and fall together: what people borrow is what people pick up. For local history the two come apart completely. A shelf of county atlases and school yearbooks circulated eleven times in 2019 and appeared in 2,300 sweep entries.

Ceri Adeyemi-Lowe, who directs the system, is careful not to overclaim. The sweep does not show that anybody read anything; it shows that an item was moved. But a collection that is moved two thousand times and borrowed eleven times is doing work of a kind the funding formula cannot see, and in 2016 that shelf had been on a list of candidates for withdrawal on the strength of its circulation alone.

What Adeyemi-Lowe wants understood is not that circulation is a bad measure. It is that circulation measures one particular behaviour — taking a thing home — and that the behaviour is spread unevenly across collections for reasons that have little to do with value. A yearbook is consulted, not read through. A county atlas does not fit in a bicycle basket. Reference material was kept non-circulating by policy for most of a century, and the habit outlived the policy by decades.

The state has not changed its formula. Kettleman still reports circulation, still runs the sweep, and publishes the two side by side with a note explaining what each one counts. Adeyemi-Lowe says the note is the part that matters, and that it took her six years to get it short enough that anyone would read it.

title: The Saxony Violin
text:
The violin came to me in a cardboard box lined with a wool coat, which was how Mr. Vasiliou moved anything he cared about. He had been my teacher for four years by then and had never once let me touch it.

“It is not a gift,” he said. “It is a loan of eighteen months. At the end you will bring it back and tell me what it taught you.” I was sixteen, and I heard only the first half.

The instrument was old and not valuable — a factory violin from somewhere in Saxony, he thought, with a repaired crack under the bass bar that made the low notes go soft in damp weather. Beside the school’s instruments it looked like a brown coat in a rack of black ones.

It was also, for the first six months, unplayable by me. Not because it was difficult. Because it was honest. My school violin had been forgiving in the way a bad microphone is forgiving: it flattened everything, the good and the bad alike, into the same pleasant nothing. The Saxony violin reported. A bow drawn a millimetre crooked came back as a scrape I could not pretend not to hear.

I spent that autumn discovering how much of my playing had been a kind of rounding. I had thought I was in tune. What I had been was close enough for an instrument that could not tell the difference.

I gave it back in the spring of my eighteenth year and told him it had taught me that I was worse than I had thought. He said that was the first half again, and waited. It took me most of another year to reach the second half, which was that for four years he had been hearing everything the school violin was hiding, and had never once said so, because he was waiting for me to have the ears to hear it for myself.

title: Ninety Words on the Wall
text:
The label beside a painting is the most-read piece of writing in any museum and the least-discussed. Visitors give the picture about eleven seconds and the label about twenty. Nobody signs it. In most institutions nobody is told who wrote it, and the writer has ninety words, give or take, in which to decide what a stranger will notice for the rest of their life.

I wrote labels for eleven years. The first thing the job teaches is that a label is not a summary; it is a door held open at a particular angle. Put the date first and the visitor reads a historical document. Put the sitter’s name first and they read a person. Put the pigment first and they read a surface. The painting does not change. The visitor’s eleven seconds change completely, and they change before the visitor knows a choice has been made on their behalf.

This is the objection my colleagues in the curatorial department raised most often, and it is a serious one. A label that steers is a label that forecloses. The purest position holds that the wall should carry the title, the artist, the date, the medium and nothing else — let the work speak. I held that position myself for about two years.

What ended it was a Tuesday in the Dutch gallery. A man in his sixties stood in front of a small winter scene for a long time and then asked me, with real embarrassment, whether it was a photograph. He was not a foolish man. He had simply never been told that anyone had painted in 1608, and the bare label — title, artist, date, medium — had told him nothing he could use. The work had spoken, and he had not been given the language.

So I stopped believing in the silent wall, and I did not start believing in the chatty one. What I came to instead was a rule I could not always keep: a label earns its ninety words only if a visitor who reads it looks back at the painting afterward. A label that sends you to the next room has failed, however elegant it is. A label that makes you look again has done the whole of its job, and it does not matter at all that nobody will ever know who wrote it.

I still test my old labels that way when I visit. Most of them fail. Two or three hold, and I stand in front of those for longer than eleven seconds, which is, I suppose, the only review a label writer ever gets.

title: The Compass in the Eye
text:
A European robin taken from a garden in Germany and released in the dark will still set off toward the southwest. Something in the bird reads the Earth’s magnetic field. What that something is has been argued over for fifty years, and the argument has been unusually productive, because the two candidate answers make predictions that pull apart under test.

The first candidate is mechanical. Tiny crystals of magnetite — the same iron oxide that makes a lodestone — were reported in the upper beak of several migratory species. A crystal small enough will twist toward north like a compass needle, and a nerve ending pressed against it would feel that twist. This is a satisfying idea because it is so concrete: a physical needle, a physical push.

The second candidate is chemical, and much stranger. In the bird’s retina sits a light-sensitive protein called cryptochrome. When a photon strikes it, two electrons can be left briefly unpaired, and the rate at which that pair settles back down depends on the angle of the surrounding magnetic field. The bird would not feel north so much as see it, as a faint pattern laid over whatever else it was looking at.

Two results moved the weight of evidence toward the retina. The first is that robins tested in total darkness lose their bearings, and so do robins under light of the wrong colour — a mechanical needle would not care about either. The second is that a weak oscillating radio-frequency field, far too feeble to move any crystal, scrambles their orientation completely. That is the signature of a chemical reaction sensitive to electron spin, and of almost nothing else.

The mechanical candidate lost further ground when the beak cells that had been taken for magnetite-bearing neurons were examined again. They were macrophages — immune cells that patrol tissue and accumulate iron as part of that work. The cells turned out to be housekeeping, not navigation, and one of the field’s most reproduced images quietly stopped meaning what it had meant.

None of this settles the whole problem, and the honest summary is narrower than the headlines. A compass and a map are not the same instrument. The retinal mechanism explains, robustly, how a bird knows which way is north. It does not explain how a bird displaced a thousand kilometres knows that it has been displaced, or in which direction, and some form of iron-based sensing may yet turn out to be doing that second job. The compass looks solved. The map does not.
